But, it creates a different experience in the lives of those in the Philippines who are born and raised there. It is, in this sense, a “global” experience, one that has a more or less universal appeal. And so the Philippines began to change, and to be changed, from one generation to the next. target: the first time in three years, according to a survey released today. The HSBC fund managers poll, which surveyed more than 1,200 fund managers in February and March and was based on a poll of managers of institutional capital, showed fund managers had a net overweight on stocks in a bear market and were more bearish on emerging market equities. A net overweight was defined as managers having more shares in positive sectors or companies, while a net bearish was defined as managers having more shares in negative sectors or companies. During the Olympic Games, the site was the venue for the opening ceremonies and the final events, in which the winning athletes were crowned as gods and goddesses. The city also boasted numerous shrines dedicated to the Olympian gods, such as the sacred temple dedicated to Hera; the Temple of Ares (the god of victory); and the Temple of Zeus (the god of victory). The Olympic Games were usually held every four years, and were considered to be one of the most sacred events of the ancient world. Over a period of two days, the population of Olympia was about 100,000. Today, the Olympic Games have been held once every four years, at the Olympic stadium in Athens, Greece.

input: Rover discovers clues of water on Mars surface After months of crossing a vast Martian crater floor and zigzagging up low-slung hills, NASA #Cassini finds two more Saturn moons NASA #39;s Cassini spacecraft has discovered two new Saturn moons, the smallest yet found among its dozens of natural satellites
target: . The spacecraft's latest pictures show the moons Enceladus and Tartarus, orbiting the planet Saturn. Enceladus is a giant ocean world with a dense atmosphere. The Saturnian moon has a large central core with two giant, liquid water reservoirs, which are exposed near the surface. Scientists believe that water is being released on the satellite as the ice is forced out with the passage of time. The picture shows a series of bright, water-covered features, some of which look like a lake-sized pool of liquid. In another photo taken in June, Enceladus is the brightest part of the image. "These moons are all incredibly interesting, and I am very pleased to see more of them. I believe this is the highest resolution of the moons to date," said Alan Stern, the principal investigator of NASA's Cassini orbiter. "We are getting amazing images and lots of new information of a world that is so far from Earth." NASA

target: -- A federal appeals court ruled Tuesday that Grokster Ltd,a travel website that enables blind people to find and book flights, has a right to access its content even if it's collected via file sharing networks. The 2-1 decision is the first of its kind. "There is a right to accessibility to copyrighted works without infringing on the copyright," Judge Frank Easterbrook wrote for the appeals court in New York, the first time a court has ruled that the right applies. target: world swimming championships in Athens, Greece, on Aug. 19, he said in a news release. He said he also received the following message from the Olympic Channel about his victory: "Congratulations Michael Phelps, your message has been received." The message is identical to a phishing email that was sent to Phelps on Friday, and it contained the same text as the message received earlier. In it, the sender asked for personal information. "After looking over this information, we have determined that it doesn't look real," Phelps' statement reads. "We do not know who sent this message or if this was a genuine message sent to the athlete. We are taking this situation very seriously and have instructed our staff to monitor Phelps' Internet activity." Phelps said the incident is being reported to the appropriate authorities. The Olympic Channel responded, saying the email was not intended for Phelps. "It's not intended for Michael Phelps and we apologize for any inconvenience," a statement reads. As Fields gets older, his health is beginning to take a greater toll. He was forced to undergo surgery in April to remove a bone spur from his left ankle, and a second operation on his right ankle in October. He went through a similar situation in the offseason last year. He's also dealing with some lingering pain in his back and hamstring. The 30-year-old is hoping to keep his career on track, but he said the first part of the season will likely be a struggle.

"What we were doing there was an atrocity, a barbarity, but we knew it was right to do it," Dr. Michael Gross, who headed a team that treated about 1,200 prisoners at a US military prison at Abu Ghraib in 2002, told the journal The Lancet. An internal US investigation, released earlier this week, concluded that "torture, in some forms, was an appropriate response" to interrogations, but that Gross and other psychiatrists played "an instrumental role in the use of abusive techniques" against detainees. The report by the Office of Inspector General concluded Gross and his colleagues at the Abu Ghraib prison provided inmates with psychological torture, and helped them to make false admissions, in order to keep prisoners from escaping. Gross was a member of a team of doctors at the prison that was supposed to treat prisoners who were under "protective custody," but instead treated those who had been captured and held for interrogation.

input: United signals it may end pensions United Airlines has signaled that it may terminate and replace employee pension plans, a move its parent company says is needed before it can emergeLayoffs at Fleet THE LAYOFFS at Fleet seem to be a microcosm of the economy as a whole. Good, higher-paying, full
target: -time jobs are hard to find. So many people are out of work that good jobs are hard to find. That's created a surplus, and some companies have decided that's a great time to cut back and fire employees. United Continental has been one of them. On Oct. 1, the airline announced that it would layoff 2,700 workers. It would not say what positions would be cut. But the company would not comment further on this week's layoffs except to say that it may no longer have a pension plan for current employees. United was among the first airlines to offer its employees defined-benefit pensions. In the 1980s and 1990s, the federal government required all large companies — including United — to offer pensions to its workers. They were able to keep them even after the companies went bankrupt or went out of business. When the government took over airlines, they were allowed to keep them until they went out of business. However, United has been growing faster than most companies.

input: Software Doesn't Break Laws... (washingtonpost.com) washingtonpost.com - What do file-sharing companies and the National Rifle Association have in common? A common legal argument, that's what.
target: This post contains some excerpts from a lengthy legal analysis on the subject. Here's a summary of the "argument": The NRA's claim that it is not breaking any laws is rooted in its belief that it is an arm of the free press, not the government. In a nutshell, this means that it should not be sued for the content of its public advocacy (its members' speeches and other public statements), even if the NRA has an obligation to keep that speech confidential. But, as we will see, it is a different law (or a very close approximation) that the companies actually have to abide by in order to protect the privacy of their members. Here are some excerpts from the article: The NRA's contention that its members do not have a duty to keep their speech confidential and should not be sued is so far from the law that it is hardly even worth discussing. The First Amendment forbids government employees from engaging in official acts that violate the rights of others.

But Margrethe Vestager, who will become the EU's top antitrust official in January, said she did not consider Gates, one of Europe's richest men, to be an "adversary" or an "anti-competitive person." "I’m not interested in wall gardens. I don’t do wall gardens," Vestager said, alluding to a proposal by Google to keep out competitors. "I’m interested in what’s best for consumers." The EU is also looking at Microsoft's practices in the U.S., where the U.S. Department of Justice is preparing an antitrust investigation. Vestager said she was concerned that the EU wasn’t getting a clear picture of how the company is doing for European customers. "We don’t have an accurate picture of how they’re actually doing in their business here in Europe," she said.

Another 3,828 complaints of irregularities were referred to other judges. "We can confirm that there is no fraud, and we have already received the results," Llodra said, before reading the results of the audit of the May 6 election. input: Thunderbird 1.0 takes on Entourage, Eudora Weeks after the launch of its Firefox 1.0 Web browser, the Mozilla Foundation on Tuesday is set to release version 1.0 of its Thunderbird e-mail client.
target: The latest release of Thunderbird is the successor to 1.0 of the e-mail client, and it aims to make it more accessible to Web users. This will include improved browsing and search capabilities as well as support for WebDAV. "Thunderbird has a long tradition of supporting the web and providing secure, convenient, and easy-to-use mail services," said Tom Webster, an adviser on Web browser development at Mozilla and Thunderbird's first director of engineering, in a statement. "We continue to work to ensure Thunderbird is a top-notch client for web mail, and we're excited to be releasing version 1.0 of the browser with many new features." Thunderbird 1.0 is available as an alpha release for test purposes now and as a beta release from Jan. 19. As with Firefox 1.0, developers and developers' organizations (D&D) have the opportunity to sign up for beta testing to participate.

input: Berlusconi hair mystery revealed by Italian surgeon (AFP) AFP - The mystery of Silvio Berlusconi's rapper-style bandana was explained when plastic surgeon Piero Rosati told the Milan daily Corriere della Sera that he had performed a hair transplant operation on the Italian prime minister.
target: Berlusconi, 71, was photographed on February 23, 2007 sporting a black bandana on his forehead. According to Rosati, who is currently president of Milan's prestigious San Raffaele Hospital, it is a sign of inflammation and has nothing to do with the hair loss he suffered in recent years. "His hair has always been thin," said Rosati in an interview, adding that he only recently heard from Berlusconi about having the operation. "I asked him to see me and then he was able to tell me the story," the plastic surgeon said. "I found him very open, he had a real will to overcome the problem," Rosati said, adding that he was pleased that the hair transplant was a success. "We can't say that he was cured because the man is still a bit swollen, but I feel I can say that he has a very good chance of recovery." - Skin

input: Hezbollah-Linked Network Ordered to Comply (AP) AP - France's highest administrative body on Friday ordered a Lebanese TV network linked to the anti-Israel group Hezbollah to adhere to broadcast regulations or face being banned from French airwaves.
target: The government-ordered decree comes as Hezbollah on Thursday issued a veiled threat to the U.S. and Israel that it could hit them with "heavy missiles." input: Hollywood to grab stardust for Nasa PASADENA (California) - Hollywood stunt pilots and Nasa scientists are teaming up to snatch a capsule full of stardust as it parachutes back to Earth next month.
target: This capsule contains the samples of the cosmic dust that fell from space when the shuttle Atlantis broke up over the Pacific Ocean in 2011. The dust could be a key ingredient in creating a space rock bigger than the Grand Canyon. "It is the first time in history that a space rock has been harvested this way for scientific study," said Tom Krier of Nasa's Planetary Science Division. With this sample capsule, the US space agency is on a mission to return not only the dust but also a rich supply of data to the research communities that study it. And the dust's origins could be of huge scientific interest. "This is a very rich source of materials, but also a lot of very fragile materials that are going to need to be handled very carefully," Krier said. The capsule will land at Nasa's Jet Propulsion Laboratory on 17 February 2012. The samples will be taken back to the lab in Pasadena, California, where scientists will take the samples to analyse.

This is Indian Country. This is where Indians grow corn. We have a big old corn planter right here. It is one of the best corn planters I've ever seen. I was amazed. The corn was all green! target: This is in comparison with the English-speaking world, where the average person has around 500,000 words in their language.The Piraha spoke to researchers of the University of São Paulo, in São Paulo, Brazil. input: Sudan, UN agree on right of return of Darfur displaced The Sudanese government and the UN migration agency here Saturday signed an agreement ensuring right of return of Darfur displaced.
target: Noting the need to return the displaced to their homes, Deputy Prime Minister Faisal Saleh Gailat told reporters at a press conference in Khartoum that the return of Darfur residents to their former lands shall begin after the signing of the agreement with the UN.Saleh said the agreement was aimed at ensuring the security and safety of the displaced and their lands and villages. "The agreement guarantees the right of return," he added, adding that the government and the UN agency signed a memorandum to this end.The UN migration agency (IOM) signed the agreement after the two sides met at the ministry in Khartoum on Saturday morning. IOM Director Anthony L. Davis said that the UN agency signed a memorandum to this end.The Sudanese government and the UN migration agency were involved in the drafting of the memorandum because the United Nations is the key organization involved in establishing of security and safety in the Darfur region.

input: Fatal accidents damage Japan #39;s nuclear dream On the coast of the Japan Sea, two and a half hours by train from Kyoto, is the quiet fishing village of Mihama. Noted for its harbour and beautiful beaches, it draws tourists from all over the country.

input: New Orleans Quarterback Aaron Brooks Tweaks Strained Right Thigh in Game Against Green Bay (AP) AP - New Orleans quarterback Aaron Brooks tweaked his strained right thigh and hobbled off the field in the second quarter of the Saints' game against the Green Bay Packers on Saturday night.
target: Saints coach Sean Payton said Brooks went on a quick cart to go to the locker room and said he had X-rays before leaving the field. Payton made it clear that there was no reason for alarm, however. Brooks had been dealing with a hamstring issue, and his status for next Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions is unclear. Brooks had completed 13 of 18 passes for 139 yards and a touchdown in the first half, and he threw two touchdown passes and one interception in the second. input: Dutch arrest in Iraq genocide case A 62-year-old Dutchman will be charged for war crimes and as an accomplice to genocide for supplying lethal chemicals to Saddam Hussein #39;s regime, prosecutors said Tuesday.
target: This is the first time that a Netherlands-trained gas expert, who later became an Iraq war criminal, has been arrested in the case. The defendant is expected to appear in court in The Hague on January 2, the prosecutors said. The man, named only as H.W., is currently in custody at a British prison and has not been formally charged. Prosecutors say they have evidence that he supplied Iraq with chemical and biological weapons in a series of contracts from the mid-1980s to the mid-1990s. Investigators say that during the 1991 Gulf War, he helped to poison Iraqi soldiers in Kuwait without the knowledge of the Iraqis themselves. Prosecutors also say the Netherlands-trained gas expert helped Iraqis kill prisoners with toxic mustard gas, including a detainee who died in 2004. Dutch prosecutors say they will demand a lengthy prison sentence when the defendant appears in court on January 2.

input: More violence ahead of Chechen election There has been more violence in the strife-torn republic of Chechnya, just days before the Russian region is due to elect a new president.
target: This comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov have been locked in a bitter feud. Two Russians, a Chechen and a former journalist, were injured as fighting broke out in the Chechen village of Tuzhnev. Two Chechen villagers said a former journalist with the Kadyrov-ruled newspaper "Dzhokhar" was killed after an altercation. According to Chechen villagers, the journalist, whose identity has not yet been confirmed by authorities, was suspected of inciting unrest in the region. Earlier this week, the journalist was detained in the village of Kura, near the town of Tuzhnev. Chechen authorities said he was suspected of inciting unrest by calling on residents to boycott a political rally in Tuzhnev. "We don't understand why they are attacking him and why they haven't killed him," one Chechen villager told Al Jazeera.

input: Violence in Iraq drives oil to new high of over $49 Oil prices raced to fresh highs Friday, carrying US crude to over $49 a barrel, driven by escalating violence in Iraq and unabated fuel demand growth from China and India.
target: This is the highest level for the oil benchmark since the start of the year, when it started to trade at around the $70 a barrel level.Oil prices were up about 0.8 percent on the day at $49.60 per barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange at 11:42 am (1442 GMT), after briefly touching $49.75 earlier, also the highest since Jan. 3. Brent crude traded up about 0.7 percent at $49.99 a barrel on ICE Futures Europe, while gasoline for February delivery jumped as much as 5 percent to the highest in more than two years.Iraqi oil officials said a bombing that targeted a U.S. military convoy killed at least four people and wounded five while the US military said its troops were being treated for injuries caused from air strikes and improvised explosive device blasts.US military personnel are "being treated and will remain in the area," said Colonel Steve Warren, a US Army spokesman.

input: College established for Internet game industry A college to provide training for the Internet games industry has been opened in Beijing. China #39;s Ministry of Information Technology, the Hong Kong Vocational Training Council, and a Beijing Internet company devised the new college as a joint venture.
target: The college was set up under the name "Xiong Xing Online Gaming Technology Center (Interactive Industry Training Center) of the Shanghai Higher Education Technology University, China #39;s largest vocational university in the field." The first class at the college begins November 8. It will provide professional training in virtual and physical game simulation technology, computer game design, and interactive industry training. "China #39;s first Internet game college has opened for business," said Li Guoli, vice-president of China #39;s Industry Ministry. "The center will further improve the country #39;s online game industry by introducing the latest technologies from all sectors in an exciting environment." The college will teach students about game simulation technologies and their use in virtual reality, as well as the latest trends in virtual reality games and other applications. "We have created a training program that will provide young people with practical business skills," said Li Hongjun, director of the college.

input: Wells of Life Run Dry for Sudanese Trauma and malnutrition leave many refugee mothers unable to breast-feed.
target: This is where support from Women’s Aid Women’s Aid is vital. Sudanese refugees are currently experiencing severe food insecurity in the Darfur region. The situation has been worsened by the recent rains – which have caused floods and caused many wells to dry, making it especially difficult to access and drink water. As these wells dry, women living in Darfur have been forced to rely on water from nearby villages, and this has led to more cases of women and children suffering malnutrition and dehydration. This situation has led to a rise in referrals for emergency malnutrition counselling services, which is a worrying development as the women and children who are suffering from acute malnutrition are often from severely disadvantaged backgrounds and cannot access services such as counselling and medicines. Women’s Aid has been providing water and sanitation services for many years in Darfur and its surrounding areas. input: Insurers Object to New Provision in Medicare Law Private insurers have told the Bush administration that they will not expand their role in Medicare if they have to serve large multistate regions.
target: This is in response to the latest provision in President Bush's health care reform law that allows Medicare to negotiate drug prices. The administration's choice of language for the provision makes clear that Medicare will not be able to extend its negotiations to the other two-thirds of private insurers if this provision is applied to them. input: Prices Fluctuate in a Flash Prices for flash memory cards -- the little modules used by digital cameras, handheld organizers, MP3 players and cell phones to store pictures, music and other data -- are headed down -- way down. Past trends suggest that prices will drop 35 percent a year, but industry analysts think
target: prices could be on the rise this year. Flash memory is made up of tiny, electrically conductive wires that are stacked to form a "flash" or "flash array." The bigger the array is, the more data can be stored. As a result, prices of flash memory products have skyrocketed over the past three years, driven higher by a surge in demand for more memory. "The memory industry is really looking to this year for the next big price drop," says Lawrence Roth, an analyst with the research group NPD. The price of flash memory is determined by the supply and demand situation, and analysts have been predicting price declines since the industry burst into the spotlight with the success of the Sony Walkman in the 1980s. "Flash prices have gone up and down and up and down," says Roth. "The prices of flash memory products have been really flat for the better part of a decade." Things are about to change.

input: Pakistan: Arrests spoil major al-Qaida plot Pakistan has arrested at least five al-Qaida-linked terrorists who were plotting suicide attacks on government leaders and the US Embassy, officials announced Saturday.
target: This is the first major detentions since last year's deadly Mumbai attacks. "This is a big breakthrough in the fight against terrorism in Pakistan," Interior Minister Rehman Malik said. input: Volkswagen #39;s Mexican Workers Accept Pay Increase, Reforma Says Mexican union workers for Volkswagen AG, Europe #39;s largest carmaker, accepted the company #39;s offer for a 6.1 percent pay increase and will return to work today after going on strike Wednesday, Reforma newspaper

input: UK takes lead role in stem cell research POTTERS BAR, England At the end of a winding country road lined with hedgerows and tidy brick homes sits a new prefabricated building chock-full of monitors and filters.
target: For all intents and purposes, this is a medical laboratory, complete with a blood bank, an ultrasound machine and a small computer with a scanner and some of the most sophisticated machines in Europe. Inside, a team of scientists is running tests on the first stem cell lines created by a new type of mouse model - mice engineered with genetic changes that make stem cells multiply in a different way than normal. "These mice are the first of their kind," says Dr. Peter McCallum, the director of the university's stem cell research institute. "They have no blood supply. input: Greek weightlifter stripped of bronze for doping In another embarrassing incident for the Olympic host nation, a Greek weightlifter has been stripped of his bronze medal for a doping offence.
target: This is the second time this year that a Greek has been stripped of a medal for a doping offence. Diarra had admitted taking the substance but blamed his mistake on the drug being mixed with a vitamin B complex called Thymoquinone. "They gave me vitamins and said they were for a doctor. They were mixed with the steroids. I took them because I had a bad cold," he said. Diarra had been selected to compete for Greece along with Olympic bronze medallist Evgenios Konstantopoulos and bronze medallist Christos Sotiridis who all tested positive for doping in July. input: Gatlin Takes 100 Meters Gold ATHENS (Reuters) - American Justin Gatlin shot to victory in the Olympic 100 meters final on Sunday in an atmosphere of fevered excitement.
target: The Olympic 100 meters final is a final on the track, and Gatlin will not compete in the 200 meters. "I'm trying to be as relaxed as I can because this is not a normal day," Gatlin told reporters after the race. "I've got to perform and this was my best race." Gatlin, 32, who had been banned by the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) for two years for doping, is one of the best sprinters in the world. The world record holder in 100 meters finished the race in 9.95 seconds with Jamaican Usain Bolt taking silver in 10.01 and Anthony Joshua of Great Britain taking the bronze, clocking 10.02.

input: Pakistan Details Suicide Attacks Plot ISLAMABAD, Pakistan Aug. 22, 2004 - Security forces hunted for more terror suspects, officials said Sunday, as Pakistan revealed it has arrested a dozen al-Qaida-linked militants planning to launch simultaneous
target: ides of suicide in three major cities. "We have arrested 12 people who were planning to attack the cities with explosives," said Lt. Gen. Mohammad Nadeem. The top military commander in Islamabad, he is in charge of military operations against the extremists, including those accused of masterminding a suicide bombing Friday that killed 25 police officers near Islamabad. Nadeem said the suspects had been in contact with militants based in Iraq. He said they planned to use a truck packed with explosives to blow up buildings in Islamabad, Rawalpindi and Karachi. And in a separate development, the Interior Minister said he will introduce a law banning the sale of liquor and other illicit substances. He said the ban will be enforced nationwide. But the minister, Shaukat Aziz, said they will not enforce a total ban on the sale of liquor and other drugs. The minister said the government has been working on the prohibition law for two years. He acknowledged the problems associated with a total ban.

input: Ramirez Hits 3-Run Homer, Cubs Beat Astros (AP) AP - Aramis Ramirez hit a three-run homer, Moises Alou also homered and the Chicago Cubs beat the Houston Astros 11-6 on Sunday in the testy conclusion of a three-game series between the NL Central rivals.
target: Ramirez had two hits and drove in three runs, and Alou homered for the second straight game as the Cubs completed a three-game sweep in the series by beating the Astros for just the fourth time since June 17. "They just played good, aggressive, good baseball," said Chicago manager Lou Piniella. "You have to be ready." Charlie Blackmon had a three-run homer, and Addison Russell added a two-run shot in a three-run ninth inning for Chicago. The Astros lost their sixth straight overall. "We played well the first two games, but we didn't compete," said Astros manager A.J. Hinch. "We've got to come out swinging." Houston led 3-0 after two innings thanks to a home run from David Freese and a solo shot from Josh Reddick. "We got a little lazy," Alou said. "Things went a little sideways."

input: Exhausted Agassi Withdraws from Long Island Tournament NEW YORK (Reuters) - American Andre Agassi has withdrawn from the TD Waterhouse Cup, starting on Monday on Long Island, citing fatigue.
target: This is Agassi's second straight absence from an event he has won eight times. "I'm tired," said the three-times major winner. "Every point, I just want to rest and come back." Agassi will be replaced by former world number one Pete Sampras in the main draw, with the tournament starting on Monday. "We don't want to take any more chances. We're going to make him play," said tournament chairman John McEnroe. "We don't want to have an athlete sit there and go through the heat without the fans, without the other players, without the coaches. We're going to make him play. "We want to make the tournament as competitive as possible for all of the participants," McEnroe added.

input: U.S. Planes Hit Militias as Tanks Near Najaf Shrine NAJAF, Iraq (Reuters) - U.S. helicopter gunships pounded Shi'ite militias in the holy Iraqi city of Najaf on Sunday as tanks rumbled to within 800 meters (yards) of a besieged
target: shrine here where the leader of Shi'ite militancy al Qaeda killed a Sunni tribal elder last month. At least three people were reported killed in the assault, which was carried out as U.S. and other air strikes had hit a separate convoy of armored vehicles entering the city. “My brother is buried there,” said Mohammed Alhazim, who identified his relative, a prominent local politician, as a member of one of the Shi'ite militias. “There is no peace here. We do not know when the security forces will go in. We pray to God for the security.” The violence in Iraq, where Sunni tribes have been arming themselves against Shi'ite militancy, threatens to derail the United States' effort to win the nation's support for its war against al Qaeda in Iraq, which is now in its eighth month and has cost over 4,000 Americans and 3,000 Iraqis their lives.

input: Tribe has great excuse for poor math skills Some people have a great excuse for being bad at math -- their language lacks the words for most numbers, US-based researchers reported on Thursday.
target: This is known as a language barrier and was previously noted in studies of Brazilian children. "We don't know why kids with a lack of words for numbers don't seem as bad as kids with a lack of words for words," said Daniel Bensam, a linguistics professor at Pennsylvania State University, who co-authored the new study published in the journal Current Biology. "We can make guesses, but it may be that there's something else going on," he said. "There may be something more complex going on," added Andrey Churcheb of the University of California, Santa Cruz. "We can't know what exactly, but we suspect it's not a bad learning disability, because this might be a symptom of something else they have," he added. input: Nigeria Wants AU Troops to Disarm Darfur Rebels Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo on Sunday proposed to give a greater role to African Union (AU) troops in restoring peace to Sudan #39;s Darfur region on the eve of talks between the Sudanese government and rebels.

input: India News: Truckers #39; strike enters second day (NIGHT LEAD) The finance minister said he suspected a role for transport booking agents in misguiding the truck operators and inciting them to go on strike.
target: This is only the second strike in nearly four years on the roads.The first was on November 30, 2017 when the BJP-led Central government had brought in the Goods and Services Tax (GST), and since then no strike has occurred. But since then, a series of protests were held on various highways across the country, with the Congress and several other opposition parties demanding a full implementation of the GST, the single biggest reform in the country, and for rollback of tax concessions granted to private companies.Union Road Transport, Highways and Shipping Minister Nitin Gadkari said that the strikes were not due to the GST. "There is no GST agitation. It is a protest against tax concessions given to companies. I believe this is due to transport booking agents and people taking a wrong decision to protest," Gadkari said."There should be a time frame for the GST rollout and those who had taken the wrong decision should be given a chance to amend this decision.

input: Fierce gunfire erupts in Najaf after mortar fire NAJAF: A fierce gunbattle erupted between US troops and radical Shi #39;ite militants near Najaf #39;s holy shrine this morning, a Reuters witness said.

input: Sony tries to win back flat-panel TV market TOKYO - Sony Corp is attempting to claw back market share of the domestic flat-panel TV market with the launch of eight new televisions.
target: This is in a country where the world's second-largest television maker has struggled for more than a decade, but the new models, including three 4K models with 120Hz (frames per second), will be aimed at a new generation of buyers, Sony said on Wednesday.The new models are among the first to be priced below 15 million yen, marking a shift in strategy for Sony as it tries to reverse a decline in sales of premium televisions.The company has not set a launch date for the new models, but did not say when they would be released. The company, which has seen its market share of flat-panel TV units drop to around 6% from more than 30% in the 1990s, has been gradually shifting its focus towards low-end and streaming products in recent years.Sony said on Tuesday that it plans to boost its share of flat panels in the global market, to between 15 and 18% in the 2020s from less than 10% in the previous decade.
